newsitem.title: USA: "Green" rules keeping U.S. hog expansion in check.
newsitem.headline: "Green" rules keeping U.S. hog expansion in check.

text.p: Tighter rules aimed at cutting odor and controlling waste at big hog farms are slowing the expansion of the U.S. hog herd at a time of booming pork exports and high prices, industry analysts said.

"There is no question that some people have found it difficult to get permits," said Steve Meyer, director of economics for the National Pork Producers Council. "Odor has been a problem more than anything else."
"Environmental concerns...I think are slowing the rate of expansion or adding to the cost of expansion," said John Lawrence, agricultural economist at Iowa State University.

The U.S. Agriculture Department last Friday estimated the U.S. hog herd as of June 1 at 58.15 million head, up two percent from a year ago. That modest increase surprised the hog industry, which had expected a greater expansion given the booming pace of pork exports this year. Industry estimates ahead of the report had indicated an expansion of between two and five percent.
Pork exports, already strong, rose further after March 20 when number two pork exporter Taiwan suddenly halted its pork exports due to an epidemic of foot and mouth disease in its hogs.
Ron Plain, University of Missouri agricultural economist, said average hog prices last year were the third highest on record and prices in 1997 may be higher.
"It looks like 1997 should beat it...and it looks like that should generate expansion," Plain said.

However, Plain agreed environmental restrictions had probably slowed expansion, noting that last week's government report estimated five to six percent more hogs will farrow, or give birth, later this year.
"Without the environmental pressures we ought to be up 10 percent (on farrowings)," Plain said.
Given the growing concentration of hog production into larger farms, regulations on odor and waste management have gotten progressively stiffer.
In Iowa, the top hog producing state, permits to build hog farms take nearly twice as long to process than three years ago.

"It's more difficult to get a site permit in the state of Iowa to build. The process has become longer and more expensive," said Mike Blaser, general counsel for Iowa Select Farms LTD, which has 60,000 sows on 55 sites in Iowa. "That has definitely slowed us down some."
Blaser said he also thought most new Iowa hog farms under construction were small ones rather than large operations.
In Fairbury, Ill., producer Roy Hankes enlarged his herd to 1,000 sows about three years ago with few problems from regulations. But he said he doubts it would be that easy now.
"There are more neighbor concerns," Hankes told Reuters.

But if expansion has been hampered in Iowa and Illinois, hog farms are expanding in some other locations and perhaps signaling a long-term shift away from the traditional center of production in the Midwest, industry analysts said.
Premium Standards Farms, a Kansas City-based hog producer, is now expanding in Texas but not in Missouri, where it already owns 80,000 sows in three counties.
"The resistance you are seeing is almost strictly a Corn Belt phenomenon," said Premium spokesman Charlie Arnot.

Premium currently has 20,000 sows in Texas and more growth there is planned because of climate, land availability and to a small degree social and political climates that are more conducive to growth.
"Most of the focus will be in Texas," Arnot said of Premium Standard's plans.
